## Task-Specific Strategies (zebralogic)
1. [Strategy: Interpret adjacency and ordering clues correctly] Handle spatial clues in three distinct ways: (a) "directly left/right of" – enforce immediate adjacency with the indicated direction; (b) "next to each other" – enforce adjacency but allow either order; (c) "somewhere left/right of" – enforce only a relative ordering without requiring adjacency.

   Example: Treating "next to each other" as a directed adjacency and fixing a direction that is not specified, leading to an impossible configuration.

2. [Strategy: Disambiguate overlapping attribute values using clue context] When a value appears in more than one attribute category (e.g., "cat" in both Animal and Pet), use cue words in the clue such as "pet", "owner", "keeps", "has", "aquarium", "enthusiast" to decide which category the clue refers to; never assume the same word always maps to the same category.
   Apply when: When processing a clue that mentions a value that exists in multiple categories.
   Example: Interpreting "cat lover" as referring to the Pet category instead of the Animal category, causing adjacency constraints to be applied to the wrong attribute.

3. [Strategy: Enforce uniqueness across each attribute category] Each value in a category must appear exactly once across all houses; after assigning a value, remove it from the candidate lists of the other houses.
   Apply when: Throughout the solving process, after any assignment.
   Example: Assigning the same pet to two different houses, violating the one‑per‑category rule.

4. [Strategy: Preserve original case of attribute values] When outputting the final solution, write each attribute value exactly as it appears in the problem statement, preserving capitalization and spelling.
   Apply when: During final answer formatting.
   Example: Changing "Peter" to "peter" or misspelling "Swede" as "Swed".

5. [Strategy: Assign fixed‑position attributes immediately] If a clue directly states that a specific attribute value belongs to a particular house number, assign that value to that house right away and remove it from all other houses.
   Apply when: Whenever a clue mentions a house number together with an attribute (e.g., "The German is in the first house").
   Example: Leaving a fixed‑position attribute unassigned and later placing it elsewhere, causing a contradiction.

6. [Strategy: Interpret distance clues correctly] When a clue says "N houses between X and Y", ensure that exactly N houses separate X and Y, i.e., |pos(X) – pos(Y)| = N + 1.
   Apply when: Whenever a clue mentions a specific number of houses between two items.
   Example: Counting the N houses as the distance itself and placing the items N houses apart instead of N + 1.

7. [Strategy: Bind equivalence clues to the same house] If a clue equates two attribute values (e.g., "The German is Eric" or "The Swedish person is Peter"), place both values in the same house.
   Apply when: When a clue directly links two attributes.
   Example: Treating "The German is Eric" as two separate statements and assigning them to different houses.

8. [Strategy: Treat 'somewhere left/right of' as inequality] Clues that say X is somewhere left/right of Y impose only an ordering (pos(X) < pos(Y) or pos(X) > pos(Y)), without requiring adjacency.

   Example: Leaving a prohibited value in a house, later causing a conflict with another clue.

10. [Strategy: Make forced assignments when only one candidate remains] If after applying all constraints a house (or an attribute) has exactly one possible remaining value, assign it immediately.
   Apply when: Whenever a domain reduces to a single option.
   Example: Leaving a single‑candidate value unassigned and later creating an inconsistency.

=== LEARNED PROBLEM-SOLVING STRATEGIES ===

## Task-Specific Strategies (zebralogic)
1. [Strategy: Interpret adjacency and ordering clues correctly] Handle spatial clues in three distinct ways: (a) "directly left/right of" – enforce immediate adjacency with the indicated direction; (b) "next to each other" – enforce adjacency but allow either order; (c) "somewhere left/right of" – enforce only a relative ordering without requiring adjacency.
   Apply when: When processing any clue that describes the relative positions of two attribute values.
   Example: Treating "next to each other" as a directed adjacency and fixing a direction that is not specified, leading to an impossible configuration.

2. [Strategy: Disambiguate overlapping attribute values using clue context] When a value appears in more than one attribute category (e.g., "cat" in both Animal and Pet), use cue words in the clue such as "pet", "owner", "keeps", "has", "aquarium", "enthusiast" to decide which category the clue refers to; never assume the same word always maps to the same category.
   Apply when: When processing a clue that mentions a value that exists in multiple categories.
   Example: Interpreting "cat lover" as referring to the Pet category instead of the Animal category, causing adjacency constraints to be applied to the wrong attribute.

3. [Strategy: Enforce uniqueness across each attribute category] Each value in a category must appear exactly once across all houses; after assigning a value, remove it from the candidate lists of the other houses.
   Apply when: Throughout the solving process, after any assignment.
   Example: Assigning the same pet to two different houses, violating the one‑per‑category rule.

4. [Strategy: Preserve original case of attribute values] When outputting the final solution, write each attribute value exactly as it appears in the problem statement, preserving capitalization and spelling.
   Apply when: During final answer formatting.
   Example: Changing "Peter" to "peter" or misspelling "Swede" as "Swed".

5. [Strategy: Assign fixed‑position attributes immediately] If a clue directly states that a specific attribute value belongs to a particular house number, assign that value to that house right away and remove it from all other houses.
   Apply when: Whenever a clue mentions a house number together with an attribute (e.g., "The German is in the first house").
   Example: Leaving a fixed‑position attribute unassigned and later placing it elsewhere, causing a contradiction.

6. [Strategy: Interpret distance clues correctly] When a clue says "N houses between X and Y", ensure that exactly N houses separate X and Y, i.e., |pos(X) – pos(Y)| = N + 1.
   Apply when: Whenever a clue mentions a specific number of houses between two items.
   Example: Counting the N houses as the distance itself and placing the items N houses apart instead of N + 1.

7. [Strategy: Bind equivalence clues to the same house] If a clue equates two attribute values (e.g., "The German is Eric" or "The Swedish person is Peter"), place both values in the same house.
   Apply when: When a clue directly links two attributes.

8. [Strategy: Treat 'somewhere left/right of' as inequality] Clues that say X is somewhere left/right of Y impose only an ordering (pos(X) < pos(Y) or pos(X) > pos(Y)), without requiring adjacency.

## Task-Specific Strategies (zebralogic)
1. [Strategy: Interpret adjacency and ordering clues correctly] Handle spatial clues in three distinct ways: (a) "directly left/right of" – enforce immediate adjacency with the indicated direction; (b) "next to each other" – enforce adjacency but allow either order; (c) "somewhere left/right of" – enforce only a relative ordering without requiring adjacency.
   Apply when: When processing any clue that describes the relative positions of two attribute values.
   Example: Treating "next to each other" as a directed adjacency and fixing a direction that is not specified, leading to an impossible configuration.

2. [Strategy: Disambiguate overlapping attribute values using clue context] When a value appears in more than one attribute category (e.g., "cat" in both Animal and Pet), use cue words in the clue such as "pet", "owner", "keeps", "has", "aquarium", "enthusiast" to decide which category the clue refers to; never assume the same word always maps to the same category.
   Apply when: When processing a clue that mentions a value that exists in multiple categories.
   Example: Interpreting "cat lover" as referring to the Pet category instead of the Animal category, causing adjacency constraints to be applied to the wrong attribute.

3. [Strategy: Enforce uniqueness across each attribute category] Each value in a category must appear exactly once across all houses; after assigning a value, remove it from the candidate lists of the other houses.
   Apply when: Throughout the solving process, after any assignment.
   Example: Assigning the same pet to two different houses, violating the one‑per‑category rule.

4. [Strategy: Preserve original case of attribute values] When outputting the final solution, write each attribute value exactly as it appears in the problem statement, preserving capitalization and spelling.
   Apply when: During final answer formatting.
   Example: Changing "Peter" to "peter" or misspelling "Swede" as "Swed".

5. [Strategy: Assign fixed‑position attributes immediately] If a clue directly states that a specific attribute value belongs to a particular house number, assign that value to that house right away and remove it from all other houses.
   Apply when: Whenever a clue mentions a house number together with an attribute (e.g., "The German is in the first house").
   Example: Leaving a fixed‑position attribute unassigned and later placing it elsewhere, causing a contradiction.

6. [Strategy: Interpret distance clues correctly] When a clue says "N houses between X and Y", ensure that exactly N houses separate X and Y, i.e., |pos(X) – pos(Y)| = N + 1.
   Apply when: Whenever a clue mentions a specific number of houses between two items.
   Example: Counting the N houses as the distance itself and placing the items N houses apart instead of N + 1.

7. [Strategy: Bind equivalence clues to the same house] If a clue equates two attribute values (e.g., "The German is Eric" or "The Swedish person is Peter"), place both values in the same house.

8. [Strategy: Treat 'somewhere left/right of' as inequality] Clues that say X is somewhere left/right of Y impose only an ordering (pos(X) < pos(Y) or pos(X) > pos(Y)), without requiring adjacency.
